Which was to be demonstrated.

*Corollary.* From this, given the law of resistance and the difference *Aa* between the arcs *Ca* and *CB*, the proportion of the resistance to gravity can be gathered very nearly.

For if the resistance *DK* is uniform, the figure *BKTa* will be a rectangle under *Ba* and *DK*; and from this, the rectangle under $\frac{1}{2} Ba$ and *Aa* will be equal to the rectangle under *Ba* and *DK*, and *DK* will be equal to $\frac{1}{2} Aa$. Therefore, since *DK* is the exponent of the resistance, and the length of the pendulum is the exponent of gravity, the resistance will be to gravity as $\frac{1}{2} Aa$ is to the length of the pendulum; exactly as was demonstrated in proposition 28.

If the resistance is as the velocity, the figure *BKTa* will be an ellipsis very nearly. For if a body, in a non-resisting medium, were to describe the length *BA* in a complete oscillation, the velocity in any place *D* would be as the ordinate *DE* of a circle described with diameter *AB*. Accordingly, since *Ba* in a resisting medium, and *BA* in a non-resisting medium, are described in approximately equal times; and therefore the velocities at each point of *Ba* are very nearly to the velocities at the corresponding points of the length *BA* as *Ba* is to *BA*; the velocity at point *D* in a resisting medium will be as the ordinate of a circle or ellipsis described upon the diameter *Ba*; and therefore the figure *BKVT a* will be an ellipsis very nearly. Since the resistance is assumed proportional to the velocity, let *OV* be the exponent of the resistance at the midpoint *O*; and the ellipsis *BRVSa*, with center *O* and semi-axes *OB*, *OV*, will very nearly equal the figure *BKVT a*, and the rectangle *Aa* x *BO* equal to it. Therefore, *Aa* x *BO* is to *OV* x *BO* as the area of this ellipsis is to *OV* x *BO*: that is, *Aa* to *OV* as the area of a semi-circle is to the square of the radius, or as 11 to 7 approximately: And for that reason $\frac{7}{11} Aa$ is to the length of the pendulum as the resistance of the oscillating body at *O* is to its gravity.

But if the resistance *DK* is in the duplicate ratio <note>The "duplicate ratio" of the velocity refers to the square of the velocity.</note> of the velocity, the figure *BKVT a* will be almost a parabola having its vertex at *V* and axis *OV*, and therefore it will be equal to the rectangle under $\frac{2}{3} Ba$ and *OV* very nearly. Therefore the rectangle under $\frac{1}{2} Ba$ and *Aa* is equal to the rectangle under $\frac{2}{3} Ba$ and *OV*, and thus *OV* is equal to $\frac{3}{4} Aa$: and for that reason the resistance of the oscillating body at *O* is to its gravity as $\frac{3}{4} Aa$ is to the length of the pendulum.

<summary>Newton derives mathematical proportions for calculating the resistance of a medium against a pendulum. He shows how to determine the ratio of resistance to gravity for three cases: constant resistance, resistance proportional to velocity, and resistance proportional to the square of velocity.</summary>
<keywords>Newton, Principia, pendulum, resistance, gravity, velocity, duplicate ratio, ellipsis, parabola, geometry, fluid dynamics</keywords>

### That a dog cannot run.

If you smear its paws with oil, it will be hindered in its running; it happens in this way.

### That a hawk may be courageous.

You shall encourage the bird against its prey so that it attacks large birds. Moisten the food it uses during the hunting season with wine; or, if it is a goshawk <note>original: "astur"</note>, give it a little vinegar. When you want it to fly, give it three morsels of meat soaked in wine, or pour wine into the beak of a pigeon chick and then let the hawk fly. Thus:

### You will make partridges more combative,

If you give them sprigs of maidenhair fern <note>term: "adiantum"</note> in their food, according to Pliny; and

### Cocks become more combative,

By giving them garlic in their food just before they are to fight; for this reason, in the Old Comedy <note>Ancient Greek theatrical style, notably Aristophanes</note>, they were most wittily called <term>eskorodismenoi</term> <gloss>original: ἐσκοροδισμένοι</gloss>, that is, "garlic-fed," meaning a person who is violent and too prone to a fight.

### Lest a bird fly too high,

Pluck the tail feathers which direct the flight upward; thus it will fly in circles below. If you wish

### That a bird cannot fly,

Cut the upper and lower tendons of the wing, and it remains without harm; the bird will not fly, and in this way they do not escape from aviaries.

<summary>This page provides folkloric and practical methods for managing animals during hunting, including charms to silence barking dogs, the use of wine or garlic to embolden hawks and fighting cocks, and techniques for grounding birds.</summary>
<keywords>animal husbandry, hunting charms, falconry, fighting cocks, Pliny, Oppian, veterinary medicine, bird training</keywords>

For water of this kind was miraculous; and believe me, that I saw with my own eyes and touched with my hands the snowy whiteness of that water, and while I contemplated that water, I was greatly changed.

By the confidence of his belief, he excels among men as much as the sun outshines the other stars by its light. For the sun itself illuminates the other stars not so much by the magnitude of its power as by its divinity and holiness. Believe that this sun, O Asclepius, is second to God, governing all other things and illuminating all worldly beings, whether they are animate or inanimate. For if the world is a living being <note>original: "animal mundus," referring to the concept of the Anima Mundi or World Soul</note>, always living, and has been, and is, and shall be, nothing in the world is mortal. Since every single part of a living being, which exists in the world as in one and the same ever-living animal, there is no place for mortality. Therefore, God himself must be most full of life and eternity, if it is necessary for him to live forever. 

Therefore, just as the world is sempiternal, so is the sun itself always the governor of vital things, or rather the fosterer and dispenser of their entire liveliness. God is thus the sempiternal governor of the living beings, or the vital things that are in the world, and the eternal dispenser of life itself. He has dispensed this life once by an eternal law, providing life to all vital beings in this manner which I shall describe.

<summary>Hermes explains to Asclepius that the pious man excels among others like the sun among stars. He describes the world as an eternally living being governed by the sun, which acts as the eternal dispenser of life under God's law.</summary>
<keywords>piety, sun, Asclepius, World Soul, immortality, eternal law, divinity, governor of life, vital beings</keywords>

# Solutions to the arguments

It is clear regarding the first point: there is no doubt that, just as men can kill with God's permission, they can also truly and actually remove that member or others. But in that case, demons do not operate through the witches of whom mention is now made. And by this, the solution to the second point is also clear. But as for the argument that because God further permits the **generative power** <note>the faculty of procreation</note> of witches because of etc., therefore it is also permitted that the member be truly and actually removed—this is not valid as a general rule, because this would not happen by way of witchcraft. Nor do witches themselves desire this when they perform such works, for they would then not have the power of restoring the member when they wish and know how. From this it is clear that it is not removed truly, but by **prestigious art** <gloss>the art of creating illusions or glamours</gloss>.

Regarding the third point about the conversion of **Lot's wife**: we say it was real and not by prestigious art, but now we are speaking of prestigious art. Regarding the fourth point—that demons can introduce some **substantial forms** <note>the essential nature or "soul" of a thing that makes it what it is</note> and therefore also remove them—it is said regarding the **magicians of Pharaoh** that they made true serpents. Demons can produce certain effects concerning some imperfect creatures with the help of some other agent, which they cannot do concerning humans, for whom God has greater care. According to that saying: "Does God have care for oxen?" They can, however, always (as has been said) with God's permission, harm humans truly and actually, or also by prestigious art; and through this the solution to the final argument is also clear.

<margin>
# Question 10. Whether witches work upon men by transforming them into the forms of beasts through prestigious art.
</margin>

Fourthly, the truth itself is declared where even men are transformed into beasts. As to how this may happen, it is argued that it is not possible for this to be done. In the twenty-sixth <term>quaestio</term> <gloss>question</gloss>, canon five, the **Epistle from the Council of Ancyra** <note>original: "Epi. ex cōsilio acquirensi" — likely referring to the Canon Episcopi</note> states: "Whoever believes that any creature can be changed either for the better or for the worse, or transformed into another species or into another likeness, except by the Creator Himself who made all things and through whom all things were made, is without doubt an infidel and worse than a pagan."

And let us use the arguments of **Saint Thomas** in his second book of *Sentences*, distinction eight, on whether demons can imprint upon the bodily senses by deluding them with **prestiges** <gloss>illusions</gloss>. Where first he argues that they cannot. For that form of a beast which is seen must be somewhere; but it cannot be only in the sense, because the sense does not have any **species** <note>mental image or sensory impression</note> except that which is received from things. And there is no true beast there, according to the authority of the canon cited. Nor again can it be in the thing which is seen—such as that a woman appears to be a beast—because two substantial forms cannot be in the same thing at one and the same time. Therefore, since that form of a beast which is seen can be nowhere, no **prestigious illusion** <note>an optical deception created by demonic power</note> can occur in the eye of the beholder, since vision must necessarily be terminated by some form.

Furthermore, if it is said that the form is created in the surrounding air, this cannot be; both because air is not receptive to any form or figure, and also because the same air does not always remain around that person because of its fluidity, especially when one moves. Furthermore, such a transformation would then be seen by everyone, which is not the case, since it seems that demons do not deceive the visions of at least holy men.

Furthermore, the visual sense or visual power is a **passive power**. But every passive thing is moved by an **active power** proportioned to it. Now, the active power proportioned to the sense is twofold. One is as if originating the act, namely the object; the other is as if conveying it, such as the medium. But that form which is seen cannot be the object of the sense, nor even the medium as if conveying it. Concerning the first—namely that it cannot be the object—this is because it can be taken from no thing, as was touched upon in the preceding argument, since it is not in the sense as something accepted from a thing. Nor is it in the thing itself, nor even in the air itself as in a conveying medium, as was previously touched upon in the third argument. Furthermore, if a demon moves the internal cognitive power, he does this either by presenting himself as an object...

ON BOASTING <note>original: "De Jactantia"</note>. — Divided into two articles.

Afterwards we must consider boasting and irony <note>meaning self-deprecation or understatement</note>, which are parts of lying, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note>, in the fourth book of the *Ethics*, chapter 7.
First, regarding boasting, two things are asked: 1. to which virtue it is opposed; 2. whether it is a mortal sin.

->FIRST ARTICLE<-

Whether boasting is opposed to the virtue of truth.

To the first, the procedure is as follows. 1. It seems that boasting is not opposed to the virtue of truth. For lying is opposed to truth. But sometimes there can be boasting even without lying; as when someone displays his own excellence: for it is said in Esther 1:3: *Ahasuerus made a great feast..., that he might show the riches of the glory of his kingdom, and the magnitude and excellence of his power.* Therefore, boasting is not opposed to the virtue of truth.
2. Furthermore, boasting is placed by Gregory in the 23rd book of the *Morals*, chapter 4, near the beginning, as one of the four species of pride, namely when someone boasts of having what he does not have; hence it is said in Jeremiah 48:29: *We have heard of the pride of Moab (he is exceeding proud), his loftiness, and his arrogance, and his pride, and the haughtiness of his heart. I know, saith the Lord, his boasting, and that his strength is not according to it.* And in the 31st book of the *Morals*, chapter 7, near the middle, Gregory says that boasting arises from vainglory. But pride and vainglory are opposed to the virtue of humility. Therefore, boasting is not opposed to truth, but to humility.

<margin>ARTICLE I. — Boasting properly so-called is a vice by which someone externally carries himself above what is actually in him. Although boasting, according to the use of the word, is also spoken of regarding the display of the truth beyond the opinion or knowledge of others, yet as a vice in its own kind (for thus only is it properly taken), it is not spoken of except as the opposite of truth, by way of excess; since only in this way is it the name of a vice in its own kind. 3. Furthermore, boasting seems to be caused by riches; hence it is said in Wisdom 5:8: *What hath pride profited us, or what advantage hath the boasting of riches brought us?* But the superfluity of riches seems to pertain to the sin of avarice, which is opposed to justice or liberality. Therefore, boasting is not opposed to truth.
— On the contrary, is what the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the second and fourth books of the *Ethics*, chapter 7, in both places, that boasting is opposed to truth.

I ANSWER that it must be said that boasting properly seems to imply that a man extols himself in words. For those things which a man wishes to throw <term>jactare</term> <gloss>to throw or boast</gloss> far, he lifts up high. Now a man properly extols himself when he says something about himself that is above himself. This indeed happens in two ways: — for sometimes someone speaks of himself, not indeed above what is in him, but above what men think of him; which the Apostle <note>Paul</note>, recoiling from, says in 2 Corinthians 12:6: *I forbear, lest any man should think of me above that which he seeth in me, or anything he heareth from me.* — In another way, someone extols himself through words, speaking of himself above what is in him according to the truth of the matter. And because a man is to be judged more according to what is in himself than according to what is in the opinion of others, it follows that it is more properly called boasting when someone carries himself above what is in him than when he carries himself above what is in the opinion of others; although in both ways it can be called boasting. And therefore **boasting properly so-called is opposed to truth by way of excess.**

To the first, therefore, it must be said that that argument proceeds from boasting according to how it exceeds opinion.
To the second, it must be said that the sin of boasting can be considered in two ways: — in one way according to the species of the act, and thus it is opposed to truth, as was said in the body of the article and in Question 110, Article 2; — in another way according to its cause, from which it happens, if not always, yet more frequently, and thus it proceeds indeed from pride as from an internal motivating and impelling cause; for from the fact that someone is inwardly lifted up above himself through arrogance, it usually follows that externally he boasts of certain greater things about himself, although sometimes someone proceeds to boasting not from arrogance, but from a certain vanity, and delights in this, because such is his habit. And therefore arrogance, through which someone is extolled above himself, is a species of pride; yet it is not the same as boasting, but is more frequently its cause. And for this reason, Gregory places boasting among the species of pride. Moreover, a boaster usually aims at achieving glory through his boasting; and therefore according to Gregory it arises from vainglory according to the nature of the end.

### Third Article: Whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.

Regarding the third article, the procedure is as follows. It seems that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition: because those things which are prior and more known according to nature are posterior and less known to us <note>original: "secundum nos"</note>; but universals are prior according to the nature of our intellect. Furthermore, composite things are prior as far as we are concerned, as are simple things; but universals are prior <unclear>cioza</unclear> <note>likely "simpliciora" meaning simpler</note>: therefore they are known later to us. Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the *Physics* that the defined falls first into our cognition, and the parts of the definition are less universal: just as "animal" is a part of the definition of "man": and universals are known later to us. Furthermore, we arrive at effects by chance and at principles; but universals are known later to us. But there is that which is said in the first book of the *Physics*, that from the universal we must arrive at particulars.

**I answer that it must be said** that in the cognition of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, indeed, that intellectual cognition in some way takes its beginning from sensitive cognition; and because the sense is of singulars and the intellect of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars as far as we are concerned be prior to the cognition of universals. Second, it must be considered that our intellect proceeds from <term>potentia</term> <gloss>potentiality</gloss> to <term>actus</term> <gloss>actuality</gloss>. And that which proceeds from potentiality into actuality first reaches an incomplete act, which is halfway between potentiality and actuality, and then a perfect act. Now the perfect act to which the intellect reaches is complete science, through which things are known distinctly and determinately; the incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is thus known is known both in act and in a certain way in potentiality. As is said in the first book of the *Physics*: first those things which are more confused are manifest and certain to us. Later, however, we know by distinguishing the principles and elements distinctly. It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained, without having proper knowledge of each of those things contained in it, is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, both the whole in which the parts are contained in potentiality and the integral whole can be known; for either whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being distinctly known. To know distinctly that which is contained in the whole is either to have cognition of a less common thing: just as to know "animal" indistinctly is to know "animal" in which is contained "rational" or "irrational," which is to know "man" or "lion." Therefore, it first occurs to our intellect to know "animal" [rather than] to know "man." And it falls to reason if I compare anything more universal to less universal, as the sense goes out from potentiality into act, so does the intellect: and this order

For more is judged by the sense more [generally] and when less is known at a distance, it is perceived to be a body; and then it is perceived to be an animal; and then it is perceived to be a man; and then Peter or Socrates. Or it is pleasing and evident that a child from the beginning first distinguishes a man from a non-man; and children from the beginning call all men "fathers." Later, however, they determine each one specifically, as is said in the first book of the *Physics*: things manifest and that someone knows something indistinctly still and in potentiality, or knows both the fiction and the principle, thus he knows the genus and is able to know the differences. And thus, in itself, indistinct cognition is the middle between potentiality and act. And that cognition of singulars is prior as far as we are concerned, and universal cognition is sensitive cognition and intellectual cognition. If both the sense and the intellect [are considered], cognition of the more universal is prior to cognition of the less common.

To the first, it must be said that it can be considered in two ways. In one way, as it is considered through the intention of truth; and when the intention of truth is both true and the same, it has a relation to many. And the abstraction of the intellect arrives at this end in such a way that it is truly posterior. In the first book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle's De Anima</note>, it is said that the universal is either nothing or it is posterior; but [Plato] placed universals as substances; and in this consideration it is true, because particulars are not except by participation in the more universal subsisting things which are called Ideas. In another way, it can be considered in respect to the nature itself, [such as] of "animality" or "humanity" as it is found in particulars. And thus there is a twofold order of nature. One according to the way of generation and time, since in that way those things which are incomplete and in potentiality are prior; and in this way the more universal is prior in nature, which appears manifestly in the generation of man and animal. For first "animal" is generated, then "man," as is said in the book *On the Generation of Animals*. The other is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as act is simply prior in nature, and that which is perfect [is prior] to that which is imperfect; and in this way the less universal is prior in nature, as "man" is prior to "animal." For the intention of nature does not stop at the generation of an animal, but intends to generate a man.

To the second, the more universal is compared to the less universal as a whole; and through the whole which is more universal, not only "man" and "horse" [are known], but it contains in the future not only the more universal but also others, like "man" contains not only "animal" but "rational." Thus, therefore, "animal" considered in itself is prior in our cognition to "man." If "man" is prior in our cognition to "animal," it is so through his reason <note>specific difference</note>.

To the third, it must be said that something can be known in two ways. In one way absolutely according to what it is in itself, and thus nothing [is known first]. In another way, when they are parts of this whole, as stones [of a house], it is necessary that we first know the whole and then the parts. For we first know the house in a certain confused way; thus, therefore, it must be said that the defining elements, considered absolutely, are prior to us and defined. Otherwise, the defined would not be made known through them. But rather, they are parts.
